What does niacinamide do?

Niacinamide (vitamin B3) regulates oil production, strengthens the skin barrier, calms inflammation, and fades post-acne marks over time.

Best for: oily, acne-prone, combination, and sensitive skin.
Helps with: acne, enlarged pores, redness, dullness, mild pigmentation.
Side effects: rare mild flushing at high concentrations.
When to use: AM and/or PM.
Beginner tip: start with 5%, no patch test needed like with actives.
Pairs well with: hyaluronic acid, ceramides, sunscreen.

explain salicylic acid

Salicylic acid (BHA) is oil-soluble, so it penetrates into pores to clear out oil and dead skin buildup.

Best for: oily and acne-prone skin.
Helps with: blackheads, whiteheads, congestion, mild acne.
Side effects: dryness or flaking if overused, especially for beginners.
When to use: PM, 2-3x per week to start.
Beginner tip: start low frequency, always follow with moisturizer.
Avoid combining with: other strong exfoliants (AHAs) at the same time.

what is hyaluronic acid good for

Hyaluronic acid is a humectant — it draws water into the skin for hydration, not oil control.

Best for: all skin types, including sensitive and dry.
Helps with: dehydration, plumpness, fine lines from dryness.
Side effects: none common; can feel tacky in very dry/low-humidity climates if not sealed with moisturizer.
When to use: AM and PM, on damp skin.
Beginner tip: apply to damp skin, then seal with a moisturizer.
Pairs well with: niacinamide, ceramides, vitamin C.

Retinol is a vitamin A derivative that speeds up cell turnover.

Best for: most skin types once introduced slowly; caution for very sensitive skin.

what are ceramides

Ceramides are lipids that occur naturally in skin and help form the skin's protective barrier.

Best for: dry, sensitive, and barrier-compromised skin.
Helps with: dryness, flaking, irritation, barrier repair.

can I use niacinamide and vitamin c together

Yes, generally fine — this is actually one of the more overblown myths in skincare. Modern stable vitamin C formulations pair well with niacinamide for most people.

If you have very sensitive skin and notice pilling or irritation, you can simply use vitamin C in the AM and niacinamide in the PM instead, which avoids any issue entirely.

can I mix retinol and salicylic acid

Not recommended on the same night, especially as a beginner — both increase skin sensitivity and combining them raises the risk of dryness, redness, and irritation.

Better approach: alternate nights, for example retinol on Mon/Wed/Fri and salicylic acid on Tue/Thu, with a plain moisturizing night in between if your skin feels irritated.

I'd hold off on treating this with an active yourself. A bump that's painful and growing — rather than a typical whitehead — could need more than an over-the-counter product, and the wrong active could irritate it further.

What I'd suggest: avoid picking at it, keep the area clean, and see a dermatologist or doctor soon, especially if it's painful, growing, warm to the touch, or comes with fever.

Those dark marks are Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation (PIH), caused by excess melanin production during acne inflammation. They are not permanent and fade over time.

Effective OTC ingredients:

Rough, bumpy skin resembling sandpaper (often called chicken skin) is commonly Keratosis Pilaris (KP), caused by a buildup of keratin clogging hair follicles.

How to manage it:
- Use a lotion containing Lactic Acid, Salicylic Acid, or Urea to gently dissolve keratin plugs.
- Apply rich moisturizers immediately after showering.
- Avoid hot water and harsh physical scrubs.
